l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Egypt was defeated by Antiochus III, who ordered his troops to stop killing the Egyptians and take them prisoner. Because of this humanity, Antiochus soon gained Pelusium and later all Egypt.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Rome received Charopes, who had been brought up there and had influence with eminent persons because of his grandfather's services. The city was also the destination toward which the expelled Ptolemy traveled.

l: Roman Senate, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: The Roman Senate forgot the Macedonians' former injuries and treated them with clemency and generosity. It allowed Perseus to live under the supervision of a keeper, freed the Macedonians, permitted the Illyrians to use their own laws, and reduced their tribute.

l: Roman conquest of Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: The Roman conquest of Macedonia followed many battles with Perseus and the overcoming of major dangers and difficulties. After gaining control of the country, the Romans proclaimed its cities free rather than reducing the population to perpetual slavery.

l: liberation of the Macedonian cities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: After conquering Macedonia, the Romans proclaimed liberty to all its cities. This generosity exceeded what the conquered peoples had expected, since they believed their former injuries had left little room for mercy.

l: Battle with Perseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: The Romans fought many battles against Perseus and overcame numerous dangers and difficulties before conquering Macedonia. Perseus's negligence, refusal to pay the Gauls, and other miscarriages contributed to the ruin of his kingdom.

l: Roman clemency toward defeated peoples, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: The Romans were described as merciful toward defeated peoples when led by noble generals. They restored Antiochus and Philip to their kingdoms after defeating them, made them allies, freed the Macedonians, allowed the Illyrians to retain their laws, and treated Perseus more mildly than his conduct deserved.

s: Antipater dies amid cruel torments and accuses Timotheus of contriving the entire scheme and persuading the young man to kill his brother. After his father's death, Philopater, surnamed Ariarathes, becomes king, celebrates the funeral with great pomp, and wins the goodwill of his subjects. Ariarathes restores Mithrobuzanes to his father's kingdom and rejects Artaxias's proposal to kill one of Mithrobuzanes's brothers and divide Sophene.

l: Antipater, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Antipater dies amid cruel torments, crying out that Timotheus contrived the entire scheme and persuaded the young man to kill his brother.

l: Asclepiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Asclepiades, governor of the city, is brought while the accusations concerning the scheme and its victims are being made.

l: Timotheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Timotheus is accused by Antipater of contriving the whole scheme and persuading the young man to kill his brother. When the great men and commanders begin to discover the design, he becomes frightened, releases the remaining condemned people from torment, and later has them secretly put to death.

l: young man (Timotheus's persuaded accomplice), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: The young man is said to have been persuaded by Timotheus to kill his brother impiously and unjustly.

l: Philopater, surnamed Ariarathes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: After his father's death, Philopater, surnamed Ariarathes, comes to the crown. He celebrates his father's funeral with great pomp, welcomes his friends, officers, commanders, and subjects, and gains the goodwill of all sorts.

l: Mithrobuzanes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Mithrobuzanes is restored by Ariarathes to his father's kingdom.

l: Artaxias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Artaxias, king of Armenia, remains infected with his old vice of covetousness and sends an ambassador to Ariarathes, urging him to help kill one of the brothers in his hands and divide Sophene.

l: Sophene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Sophene is the territory that Artaxias proposes to divide with Ariarathes after they kill one of the brothers in his hands.

l: Mithrobuzanes's father's kingdom, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Mithrobuzanes's father's kingdom is restored to Mithrobuzanes by Ariarathes.

l: Antipater's death by torment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Antipater's death occurs amid cruel torments, during which he accuses Timotheus of responsibility for the scheme.

l: Philopater's father's funeral, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Philopater's father's funeral is celebrated with great pomp and state after Philopater comes to the crown.

l: Timotheus's design and contrivance, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Timotheus's design and contrivance are exposed when the great men and commanders begin to discover the whole scheme and pity those subjected to cruel torments.

l: the killing of the brother, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: The young man kills his brother after being persuaded by Timotheus; Artaxias later urges Ariarathes to participate in another killing of one of the brothers in his hands.

l: Ariarathes's restoration of Mithrobuzanes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 7 1 Antipater having breathed out hU last m the midsC of thete
s: Ariarathes restores Mithrobuzanes to his father's kingdom, and Mithrobuzanes regains it through Ariarathes's faithfulness and integrity.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus and was consul and censor, died and received an exceptionally well-attended funeral at Rome. Although he had controlled immense wealth and authority, he left so little private property that his adopted sons had to sell land to pay his wife's dowry. His natural son Publius Scipio, adopted into the family of Scipio Africanus, studied Greek learning and philosophy and became renowned for sobriety, virtue, generosity, chastity, and courage. Publius Scipio distributed inheritances and money generously among his mother, sisters, and brother, and later surpassed the Macedonian kings in hunting.

l: Lucius Aemilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: Lucius iEmilius conquered Perseus and was consul and censor. He was regarded as the bravest man of his age among the Romans, and his death caused widespread sorrow. Although he controlled great wealth and authority in Spain and Macedonia, he did not convert it to private use; after his death, his adopted sons had to sell land to pay his wife's dowry.

l: Publius Scipio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: Publius Scipio was the natural son of Lucius iEmilius and the adopted son of Scipio, who conquered Hannibal and the Carthaginians. He studied Greek learning and philosophy under Polybius of Megalopolis and became known for sobriety, affability, generosity, chastity, courage, and other virtues. He gave inheritances and money to his mother, sisters, and brother, paid dowries in full at once, helped fund his brother's funeral games, and surpassed the Macedonian kings in hunting.

l: Scipio Africanus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: Scipio Africanus, who conquered Hannibal and the Carthaginians, was the adoptive grandfather of Publius Scipio. He is described as the most eminent of all the Romans who had lived before him.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: The Romans of the earlier period are presented as capable of sobriety, moderation, and freedom from covetousness, unlike Romans of the author's time, who are said to exceed other nations in insatiable desire for riches. Roman youths of the period described were widely drawn toward lust, intemperance, drunkenness, revelry, and luxury.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: Rome received the remains and funeral honors of Lucius iEmilius. The senate, magistrates, common people, and inhabitants of neighboring free towns and cities gathered there for the funeral.

l: funeral of Lucius iEmilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: The funeral of Lucius iEmilius drew artificers, common people, the senate, magistrates, and people from neighboring free towns and cities. The widespread attendance reflected the general sorrow and lamentation caused by his death.

l: philosophy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: Publius Scipio began studying philosophy at eighteen under Polybius of Megalopolis, the historian, who was his tutor. His study was associated with his growth in virtue and his distinction from those who had previously considered him dull and unworthy of his family.

l: virtue, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: Publius Scipio increased in virtue and surpassed both his equals and those older than himself in sobriety, affability, generosity, and other commendable qualities. His conduct made him worthy of the renown of his ancestors.

l: sobriety and temperance, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: Publius Scipio made sobriety his chief concern in youth and struggled against his natural lusts and the prevailing intemperance around him. Within five years he attained a fixed and habitual state of sobriety and temperance, which contributed to his reputation, health, and bodily strength.

l: generosity and liberality, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 74. Lucius iEmilius, who conquered Perseus, and was fi consul
s: Publius Scipio displayed generosity and liberality by giving his inherited wealth to his mother, sisters, and brother, paying dowries immediately, and sharing the expense of his brother's funeral games. His reputation rested especially on choosing suitable opportunities and proper recipients for his gifts and benefits.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: The unit describes abuses by rulers and commanders, including Charopes, Orophernes, Prusias, the counterfeit Philip, and Demetrius of Syria. It contrasts these acts with the clemency and humanity shown by Philip son of Amyntas, Alexander son of Philip, the Romans, Publius Scipio Africanus, and Caius Julius Caesar. It also recounts Roman conquests and destructions involving Greece, Corinth, Carthage, Macedonia, and other regions. Several episodes present sacrilege, treachery, and broken faith as followed by punishment or failure.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: The Romans executed some Macedonian partisans after conquering Perseus and sent others to Rome. They expanded their power largely through warfare but also through clemency toward conquered peoples, making some free of the city, arranging marriages, allowing others to retain their laws, and winning the protection of kings, cities, and countries. After becoming lords of much of the world, they also used severity and destroyed Corinth, Carthage, Numantia, and the kingdom of Macedonia to terrify their enemies.

l: Orophernes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Orophernes deposed his brother Ariarathes and pursued money rather than governing prudently or winning the goodwill of his people. He put many to death, paid large sums to Timotheus and Demetrius, robbed and confiscated the goods of the Cappadocian nobility, and deposited four hundred talents with the Pirenians. When his affairs declined, he robbed Jupiter's temple to pay his mercenary soldiers.

l: Prusias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Prusias, king of Bithynia, destroyed the sacred grove of Nicephorius, plundered its temple, and removed its statues, images, and treasures after failing to capture Attalus. He was then punished when much of his land army died from the bloody flux and much of his naval force was destroyed by a storm in the Propontis.

l: Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Philip son of Amyntas liberated a kingdom subject to the Illyrians and enlarged his kingdom through military skill and mild treatment of those he conquered. After defeating the Athenians, he buried their dead and returned more than two thousand prisoners without ransom, leading his former enemies to yield him the sovereignty of Greece. He later maintained his gains by destroying Olynthus and striking fear into his enemies.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Greece was contested by Philip son of Amyntas and the Athenians, who fought over its principality. The Athenians eventually yielded sovereignty over Greece to Philip after hearing of his generous treatment of their fellow citizens.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Alexander son of Philip deterred the Lacedaemonians and Athenians from revolt by destroying Thebes. In the Persian war, his civil and generous treatment of prisoners won the hearts of the Asiatics through mildness and humanity as well as valor.

l: Corinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Corinth in Achaia was utterly destroyed by the Romans. Almost a hundred years later, Caius Julius Caesar saw its ruins and undertook to rebuild the city.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Carthage in Africa was utterly destroyed by the Romans. After its capture, Publius Scipio gave the Sicilian ambassadors permission to search its spoils and recover objects previously taken from their cities.

l: Scipio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Publius Scipio, later surnamed Africanus, kept his promises to besieged enemies when other Romans disregarded their sworn agreements and treated those who fell into his hands with humanity and clemency. His reputation for faith and integrity became so great in Africa that people surrendered to the Romans only when he joined in signing the articles. He also requested that Asdrubal bury three Romans killed in a skirmish, and Asdrubal complied.

l: Caius Julius Caesar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Caius Julius Caesar, surnamed Divus, was moved by compassion when he saw the ruins of Corinth and tried to rebuild the city. The text praises his humanity, clemency, moderation, eloquence, military skill, birth, and contempt for riches.

l: Syria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Syria was brought low while Demetrius was the only surviving branch of the royal stock. The rival royal families' plots and the people's attraction to changing rulers kept Syria full of disturbances.

l: Demetrius of Syria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Demetrius of Syria became increasingly intolerable and cruel, encouraged by a wicked friend who flattered him. He executed opponents, murdered Antiochians and their families, burned much of Antioch, confiscated estates, and drove many citizens into exile; he was hated by everyone and exceeded his father in cruelty.

l: Roman clemency toward defeated peoples, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: Roman clemency toward conquered peoples helped enlarge Roman conquests because the Romans treated many conquered people as friends rather than enemies. They made some free of the city, joined others to themselves by marriage, and allowed others to govern under their own laws. Later, after gaining dominion over much of the world, they combined clemency with severity and the destruction of cities to secure their rule.

l: warfare and conquest, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 77* After the Romans had conquered Perseus, (orratherCbaropea),
s: The unit presents warfare and conquest as being secured both by force and by humane treatment. Philip son of Amyntas, Alexander son of Philip, and the Romans gained or maintained power through a mixture of military victories, clemency, and, when needed, the destruction of rebellious or hostile cities.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: The unit describes the cruelty of Ptolemy Physcon in Egypt, the virtues and death of Viriathus among the Lusitanians, and the atrocities of Diegylis in Thrace. It recounts the conduct of Viriathus at his marriage and the honors given at his burial. It also relates Pompey's capture of Lagnetia after the Lagnetians turned against their Numantian auxiliaries. The text further records the reactions of the Egyptians, the actions of Attalus, and the conduct of Ptolemy's general Hierax.

l: Ptolemy Physcon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: Ptolemy Physcon began his reign by executing people accused of plotting against him, banishing others on invented charges, and confiscating their estates. He was hated for his cruelty, murders, filthy lusts, childish speeches, intemperance, and deformed body; his general Hierax eventually took over the government when soldiers threatened to revolt.

l: Viriathus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: Viriathus despised luxury, valued sobriety and temperance, and regarded the liberty of his country won by valor as the surest possession. He was faithful in treaties, honest in speech, vigilant and courageous as a commander, and beloved by his soldiers because he shared spoils fairly and aided those in need.

l: Diegylis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: Diegylis ruled his people tyrannically, treating them as slaves, plundering neighboring Greek cities, and committing many murders and abuses. His subjects hated him for his cruelty and covetousness, while Attalus gained praise by treating captives and refugees generously.

l: Attalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: Attalus took a course contrary to Diegylis by releasing Thracian prisoners and receiving Thracian nobles who fled from Diegylis. His generosity and clemency became widely known.

l: Pompey, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: Pompey besieged Lagnetia and demanded that the Numantians be surrendered. After the Numantians attacked the Lagnetians, Pompey captured the city, put its citizens to the sword, released the Numantian auxiliaries, and razed the city.

l: Numantians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: The Numantians sent four hundred soldiers to assist their countrymen in Lagnetia. When the Lagnetians planned to surrender them to Pompey, the Numantians attacked the citizens by night; after the city's capture, Pompey released the surviving Numantian auxiliaries.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: The Egyptians hated and condemned Ptolemy because of his cruelty, childish speech, filthy lusts, and body weakened by intemperance.

l: Thracians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: The Thracians suffered under Diegylis, who tortured, mutilated, killed, and abused many of them. Some Thracian nobles fled to Attalus, who received them kindly.

l: Lusitanians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: The Lusitanians regarded Viriathus as an exceptionally successful and beloved commander. They buried him with great pomp, including gladiatorial combats at his sepulchre, and after his death their forces were soon broken and dispersed.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: In Egypt, Ptolemy was hated by his subjects, who contrasted his fierce and cruel character with the mild nature of his brother Philometor. The people longed for a change and awaited an opportunity to revolt.

l: Thrace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: Thrace was ruled by Diegylis, who filled his dominions with rapine and violence and plundered neighboring Greek cities.

l: Ptolemy Physcon's reign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: Ptolemy Physcon's reign began most wickedly with executions, torture, banishments, and confiscations. Despite the hatred these actions provoked, he reigned for fifteen years.

l: Viriathus's marriage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: At Viriathus's marriage, he mocked the displayed gold, silver, and rich carpets by holding them on a lance. He ate only bread and flesh, sacrificed according to the manner of the Spaniards, and carried his bride on horseback to his mountain apartments.

l: Siege of Lagnetia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: During Pompey's preparations to besiege Lagnetia, the Numantians sent four hundred soldiers to aid the city. The Lagnetians first welcomed and rewarded them but later sought terms with Pompey and considered surrendering their benefactors.

l: Capture of Lagnetia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: The Numantians attacked the Lagnetians after learning of the proposed betrayal. Pompey then scaled and captured the city, killed the Lagnetians, released the Numantians, and later razed the city.

l: Viriathus's burial, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: The Lusitanians buried Viriathus with great pomp and honor. Two hundred gladiators fought against two hundred others in single combats at his sepulchre.

l: Ptolemy's cruelty and tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: Ptolemy's cruelty and tyranny included killing people on accusations of plots or invented crimes, banishing them, confiscating their estates, and ordering executions even during celebrations. His conduct caused his subjects to hate him and desire revolt.

l: Viriathus's virtues, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: Viriathus was described as sober, temperate, honest, faithful to treaties, courageous, prudent, vigilant, and generous to his soldiers. He shared spoils without taking more than others, rewarded bravery, relieved the needy, and remained unconquered while commanding the Lusitanians.

l: Diegylis's atrocities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 98. Ptolemy Physcon, the brother of Philometor, began hb
s: Diegylis's atrocities included torture, murder, rape, plunder, mutilation, crucifixion, and the dismemberment of captives and hostages. At his wedding he had two beautiful Greek brothers prepared as sacrificial victims, then killed both when the elder tried to protect the younger.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: A massive slave mutiny in Sicily erupted after prolonged exploitation, cruelty, and unchecked violence by slaveholders, bringing many cities and the island itself near collapse. Similar unrest occurred in Asia, where slaves joined Aristonicus and helped fill towns and cities with bloodshed. Damophilus of Euna and his wife Megallis exemplified extreme cruelty toward slaves, while their daughter was spared because she had treated abused servants kindly. Eunus became king after the revolt, Cleon led another slave rebellion around Agrigentum, and Attalus's cruelty in Asia helped provoke opposition to his rule.

l: slave mutiny and sedition in Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: A vast and unexpected slave mutiny broke out in Sicily, with many cities ransacked, countless people suffering, and the whole island nearly falling into the hands of the slaves. The revolt arose after growing cruelty by masters and hatred among the slaves.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Sicily was overwhelmed by slave unrest, robbery, murder, and disorder. Its wealthy inhabitants maintained large numbers of harshly treated slaves, while Roman pretors and governors were unable to suppress the abuses effectively because powerful Roman slaveholders could influence judicial proceedings.

l: rebellious slaves, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Many thousands of slaves in Sicily suddenly united against their masters, and their revolt brought cities and the countryside into violence. Some slaves became armed shepherds and herdsmen who robbed travelers, attacked villages, and killed those who resisted; others followed Eunus or Cleon.

l: slaveholders and masters in Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Slaveholders bought whole gaols of prisoners to work their lands, overburdened them with labor, branded them, and often denied them adequate clothing, food, wages, and subsistence. Their cruelty and reliance on powerful connections prevented magistrates from punishing the slaves' abuses and helped produce the revolt.

l: Aristonicus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Aristonicus sought to gain the kingdom of Asia without any stated right. Slaves joined him because of their masters' cruelty, and together they filled many towns and cities with bloodshed.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Asia experienced a slave uprising at nearly the same time as Sicily. Slaves joined Aristonicus, while the later cruelty of Attalus caused subjects and neighboring nations to seek a change of government.

l: Damophilus of Euna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Damophilus was a wealthy, proud, and arrogant landowner of Euna who possessed extensive land and cattle and imitated the luxury and cruelty of Italian slaveholders. He armed and displayed slaves, held lavish entertainments, branded captives, imprisoned some, denied others sufficient clothing and food, and scourged slaves almost every day; his treatment provoked them to revolt.

l: Megallis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Megallis, the wife of Damophilus, was as cruel as he was toward maidservants and other slaves under her control. Her abuse contributed to the slaves' decision to rise up.

l: Eunus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Eunus was declared king during the Sicilian slave revolt. He put many people to death but spared those who had previously praised his prophecies at feasts or had shown him kindness by sharing food with him.

l: Cleon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Cleon was a Sicilian near Mount Taurus who had practiced robbery from boyhood while tending horses. After hearing of Eunus's success, he persuaded neighboring slaves to join him, revolted, and plundered Agrigentum and the surrounding country.

l: Attalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Attalus, newly come to the throne in Asia, ruled differently from his predecessors and was cruel and bloodthirsty. Suspecting powerful relatives and associates of plotting against him, he arranged their murders along with those of their wives and children, causing his subjects and neighboring nations to seek his overthrow.

l: luxury and moral corruption, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: The inhabitants of wealthy Sicily became excessively comfortable and indulgent through abundant prosperity, then fell into pride and insolence. This moral decline accompanied the worsening cruelty of masters and helped create the conditions for the slave revolt.

l: cruelty of masters toward slaves, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Cruelty by masters in Sicily increased steadily through branding, forced labor, inadequate food and clothing, withheld subsistence, imprisonment, and frequent scourging. The text presents this cruelty as a principal cause of the slaves' hatred and rebellion, and it likewise helped drive slaves in Asia to join Aristonicus.

l: slave labor and exploitation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Large landowners in Sicily bought prisoners and used them as agricultural laborers and shepherds, imposing severe work while denying adequate support and wages. Some Italian slaveholders allowed armed shepherds to rob because they would not provide necessary subsistence, turning exploited workers into organized bands of violent raiders.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, .16. Atheneus, Antiochu^'s general, in a short time met with a
s: The unit describes the punishments and fortunes of several rulers, generals, and Roman statesmen. Caius Gracchus is killed by his servant, while Lucius Vitellius betrays him for a reward. Jugurtha defeats and kills his brother Adherbal despite Roman intervention. Publius Scipio Nasica is praised for his virtue and political judgment, including his argument that Carthage should be preserved; later, his son kills Tiberius Gracchus.

l: Caius Gracchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, .16. Atheneus, Antiochu^'s general, in a short time met with a
s: Caius Gracchus was killed by the hands of his own servant. Lucius Vitellius cut off his head and brought it to Lucius Opimius in exchange for its weight in gold.

l: Jugurtha, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, .16. Atheneus, Antiochu^'s general, in a short time met with a
s: Jugurtha routed the Numidians in a great battle and besieged his brother Adherbal in Cirta. He ignored Roman orders to raise the siege, forced the city to surrender through famine, killed Adherbal, and scourged to death the Italians who had aided him.

l: Adherbal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, .16. Atheneus, Antiochu^'s general, in a short time met with a
s: After Jugurtha defeated him, Adherbal fled to Cirta and was besieged there. He appealed to Rome for help, but Jugurtha disregarded the Roman embassies, captured the city, and killed him as he was leaving with his children.

l: Publius Cornelius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, .16. Atheneus, Antiochu^'s general, in a short time met with a
s: Publius Scipio Nasica was renowned for virtue, noble birth, piety, prudence, and political judgment. The senate judged him the best man among the Roman citizens, and he argued that Carthage should be preserved because its continued existence would restrain Roman pride and preserve peace.

l: Roman Senate, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, .16. Atheneus, Antiochu^'s general, in a short time met with a
s: The Roman senate sent successive embassies ordering Jugurtha to raise his siege of Cirta, but he disregarded them. It also judged Publius Scipio Nasica the best man among the Roman citizens and followed the Sibyl's instructions concerning the reception of the Great Mother's image.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, .16. Atheneus, Antiochu^'s general, in a short time met with a
s: Carthage was the subject of disagreement between Marcus Cato, who repeatedly urged that it be destroyed, and Publius Scipio Nasica, who argued that it should be preserved. The text says that after its destruction, Roman factions, revolts, civil wars, and hostility from allies followed.

l: Tiberius Gracchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, .16. Atheneus, Antiochu^'s general, in a short time met with a
s: Tiberius Gracchus was killed by Nasica when he was attempting to establish himself as ruler. Although the people were angered by the murder, they became quiet after Nasica openly admitted the deed and asserted that Gracchus had sought absolute monarchy.

l: Caius Marius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, .16. Atheneus, Antiochu^'s general, in a short time met with a
s: Caius Marius was slighted by the proconsul as one of the least important ambassadors because he was said to have been a publican. He devoted himself to military affairs, became an expert and famous soldier, won the affection of his soldiers through generosity and courtesy, and led the Romans to victory when he commanded them.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: The slave revolt and general lawlessness devastated Sicily, where rebellious slaves and impoverished free people committed widespread robbery, murder, and destruction in the absence of a Roman praetor. Saturninus was rebuked and removed from office by the Roman Senate for mismanaging the grain supply, but later became tribune of the people after reforming his way of life. The Roman people recalled Metellus from banishment after his son repeatedly pleaded for him, despite reluctance to establish a precedent for restoring exiles. The unit contrasts Roman luxury and moral corruption with the just provincial administrations of Quintus Mutius Scaevola, Lucius Asellius, and their associates, and concludes by introducing the young Marcus Livius Drusus.

l: rebellious slaves, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: The rebellious slaves devastated Sicily, robbed towns, villages, barns, and travelers, drove away herds, killed people without distinction between slaves and free persons, and made the highways impassable. Slaves remaining within the cities were feared by their masters because they longed for an opportunity to revolt.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Sicily was ravaged by rebellious slaves, bandits, and impoverished free people. With no Roman praetor exercising jurisdiction, its cities, towns, and countryside suffered widespread anarchy, robbery, violence, and the collapse of law and justice.

l: Saturninus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Saturninus, described as having lived extravagantly, ordered all the grain from the province of Ostia to be carried to Rome. The Roman Senate rebuked him for maladministration, stripped him of authority, and replaced him, but after becoming sober in conduct he was later chosen tribune of the people.

l: Roman Senate, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: The Roman Senate rebuked Saturninus for mismanaging the province of Ostia, deprived him of his authority, and entrusted the province to another administrator.

l: Metellus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Metellus was restored from banishment after the Roman people were moved by the persistent appeals of his son. His recall was debated in public assemblies for two years.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: The Roman people were reluctant to establish a precedent for restoring exiles contrary to the laws, but compassion for Metellus's son and his repeated entreaties led them to recall Metellus from banishment.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Rome received the grain ordered away from the province of Ostia by Saturninus. The city is also described as a place where luxury, prodigality, and extravagant living became more valued than military service or sober conduct.

l: Quintus Mutius Scaevola, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Quintus Mutius Scaevola served as proconsul in Asia and used his own virtuous example to reform corrupt manners. He paid the expenses of himself and his retinue, governed moderately and justly, protected the province from oppression, suppressed false accusations, and punished abusive publicans.

l: Quintus Rutilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Quintus Rutilius was chosen by Quintus Mutius Scaevola as his legate in Asia. Scaevola relied on his advice in administering the government and making laws.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Asia had previously suffered oppression and illegal exactions from proconsuls allied with the publicans. Under Quintus Mutius Scaevola's administration, it was freed from those miseries through moderation, justice, and the punishment of abusive tax gatherers.

l: publicans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: The publicans had filled Asia with oppression through illegal exactions and abuses. Quintus Mutius Scaevola restrained them, had injured people compensated, and imposed fines or death sentences for offenses according to their severity.

l: Roman knight Publius Rutilius Rufus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: The Roman knight Publius Rutilius Rufus served as Lucius Asellius's counsellor in Sicily and resided at Syracuse. He was notable for piety toward the gods, sobriety and temperance, learning, courtesy, and generosity toward students of the liberal arts.

l: Lucius Asellius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Lucius Asellius was sent as praetor to Sicily and found the province greatly devastated. With the assistance of Caius Sempronius Longus and Publius Rutilius Rufus, he reformed its administration, protected the poor and vulnerable, suppressed false accusers and injuries, and restored the province to prosperity.

l: Caius Sempronius Longus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Caius Sempronius Longus was chosen by Lucius Asellius as his legate in Sicily. He lived under the same roof as Asellius and joined him and Publius Rutilius Rufus in advising and judging the province.

l: Marcus Livius Drusus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Marcus Livius Drusus was very young but was praised for his physical and mental qualities. He was eloquent, wealthy, faithful to his word, influential among the citizens, courageous, and regarded as the principal patron of the senate.

l: luxury and moral corruption, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: After Rome had conquered many nations and enjoyed prolonged peace, its people declined from military virtue into luxury and moral corruption. Extravagant feasts, costly furnishings, fine wines, luxurious clothing, expensive cooks, and enslaved boys were widely desired, while wealth and indulgence were treated as signs of happiness.

l: public administration and justice, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Public administration and justice were severely disordered in Sicily during the slave revolt, while provincial governors and tax collectors often oppressed the inhabitants. Quintus Mutius Scaevola and Lucius Asellius are presented as restoring justice through personal frugality, impartial judgments, protection of the weak, and punishment of abuses.

l: slave mutiny and sedition in Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: The slave revolt in Sicily expanded into widespread devastation, robbery, murder, and insecurity affecting both slaves and free people. The absence of a Roman praetor allowed lawlessness to spread through the cities, towns, countryside, and highways.

l: Metellus's recall from banishment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Metellus's recall from banishment followed two years of public debate and the repeated pleas of his son, who appeared before citizens with unkempt hair and beard, tears in his eyes, and a torn garment. The Roman people granted the recall out of compassion despite concerns about violating the laws and setting a precedent.

l: Roman provincial reform, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVI.
s: Roman provincial reform is exemplified by Quintus Mutius Scaevola in Asia and Lucius Asellius in Sicily. Both relied on trusted advisers, paid their own expenses, resisted corruption and false accusations, protected the oppressed, and used justice and personal example to restore their provinces.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Pompoedius led armed Marsi and other men toward Rome to demand citizenship, but Caius Domitius persuaded him to approach the Senate peacefully, preventing violence. Lucius Sylla gained renown through military achievements, while Mithridates won support in Asia by treating Roman prisoners leniently. Gaius Marius’s greed helped provoke civil wars and severe calamities in Italy, including proscriptions and mass killings. Fimbria encouraged plunder and violence, whereas Cn. Pompeius distinguished himself through discipline, military training, and victory over Junius Brutus.

l: Quintus Pompoedius Silo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Pompoedius, a general of the Marsi, marched toward Rome with armed men, intending to surround the Senate, demand the city’s freedom, and use fire and sword if necessary. Caius Domitius persuaded him to return home and seek the favor of the Senate through petitions rather than hostility.

l: Caius Domitius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Caius Domitius met Pompoedius on the road and advised him to approach the Senate peacefully and respectfully. His prudent speech turned Pompoedius back and delivered Rome from threatened violence.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Rome was threatened by Pompoedius and his armed followers, who considered laying the city waste if their demands were rejected. It later suffered civil violence, proscriptions, killings, and other calamities during the conflicts involving Marius and Sylla.

l: Roman Senate, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: The Senate of Rome was the intended target of Pompoedius’s armed demonstration. Caius Domitius argued that it should be petitioned rather than compelled to grant favor to the Latins and their allies.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: The Roman people judged Lucius Sylla worthy of the consulship because of his valor and military conduct. They also condemned Gaius Marius to death, although he escaped by flight.

l: Lucius Sylla, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Lucius Sylla gained great fame through brave and distinguished military actions and was regarded as likely to attain the highest glory. He robbed the temples of Apollo at Delphi, Esculapius at Epidaurus, and Jupiter at Olympus to obtain money for war, later claiming that the gods assisted him because they had supplied him with funds.

l: Mithridates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Mithridates, after defeating Roman generals in Asia, sent Roman prisoners home clothed and supplied with provisions. His clemency won widespread praise, and many cities welcomed him as a god and deliverer.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Asia saw Mithridates’s party sweep aside Roman resistance, causing cities to revolt from the Romans. The Lesbians surrendered themselves to Mithridates and attempted to deliver Aquilius to him.

l: Caius Marius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Gaius Marius was renowned in his youth for ambition, courage, freedom from covetousness, and achievements in Europe and Africa. In old age he coveted the wealth of Mithridates and Asia and sought Cornelius Sylla’s province, bringing calamities upon himself and contributing to the civil wars and destruction in Italy.

l: Cornelius Sylla, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Cornelius Sylla was assigned a province that Gaius Marius unlawfully sought to have transferred to himself. The text later describes Sylla as bringing a dreadful war upon Rome.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Italy was afflicted by wandering, poverty, civil war, slaughter, and widespread destruction. Its people and cities suffered after the conflicts involving Marius and Sylla, while Marius’s son also perished after the capture of a city.

l: civil wars, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: The civil wars in Rome enabled Gaius Marius to return after exile and join those judged enemies of the Romans. They produced proscriptions, murders of eminent men, the slaughter of much of the Senate, and the deaths of many soldiers.

l: Cinna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Cinna agreed to peace on the condition that he be restored to the consulship. Lucius Cornelius Merula surrendered his consulship so that Cinna could receive it, after which the Senate’s ambassadors brought Cinna into the city.

l: Fimbria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Fimbria encouraged his soldiers to plunder allied territories, seize captives, extort cities, and keep the wealth they acquired. He used violence at Cyzicum, executing prominent citizens and forcing others to pay ransoms, while his permissiveness won the soldiers’ loyalty.

l: Cneius Pompeius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVII.
s: Cn. Pompeius trained himself rigorously for military service, enduring a spare diet, little sleep, and constant study of military affairs. He quickly trained and disciplined an army, and after defeating Junius Brutus he became recognized for his military ability.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The unit describes Roman diplomatic and military dealings with the Albani, Grecians, Antiochus, the Aetolians, Perseus, and various rulers and cities of Asia. Rome negotiated peace with Antiochus on severe terms, including territorial concessions, tribute, surrender of elephants and ships, and the delivery of Hannibal and others. After victories over Antiochus, Roman commissioners redistributed territories in Asia and continued directing the affairs of Greece and neighboring kingdoms. The Roman Senate later declared war against Perseus, received embassies from many states, investigated Eumenes, and sharply rebuked the submissive Prusias.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Romans claimed to pursue just and defensible wars, as shown by their treatment of the Alban ambassadors. They demanded that Antiochus abandon his claims in Europe and accept extensive terms after the war, and they continued to direct the political arrangements of Greece and Asia.

l: Albani, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Albani falsely accused the Romans of thefts and robberies and sent ambassadors to demand justice while threatening war. After Roman ambassadors were denied justice at Alba, the Albani became enemies of Rome.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Rome received embassies from the Albani, Grecians, Antiochus, the Aetolians, Asian states, Rhodes, and other rulers. Its Senate used these audiences to negotiate settlements, impose conditions, encourage allies, and declare war against Perseus.

l: Nabis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Ambassadors from Nabis and Flamininus came to Rome concerning the terms of peace. The Senate confirmed the articles and ordered the removal of garrisons and the withdrawal of forces from Greece.

l: Titus Quinctius Flamininus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Flamininus summoned the Greek nobility and explained that Greece would be free from garrisons and governed by its own laws, while asking that Italian servants be discharged. In negotiations with Antiochus, he presented the Roman alternatives concerning Antiochus's claims in Europe and Rome's support for its allies.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Grecians were told by Flamininus that they would be free, relieved of garrisons, and governed by their own laws. Their ambassadors applauded the Senate's position against Antiochus and were encouraged to continue the war against him.

l: Antiochus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Antiochus sought peace with Rome, first offering to bear half the war's expenses and surrendering several cities, and later asking pardon on any terms. He accepted a settlement requiring him to abandon Europe and territories on the Roman side of the Taurus, surrender his elephants and long ships, pay fifteen thousand Euboean talents, and deliver Hannibal, Thoas, and others.

l: Europe, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Roman Senate demanded that Antiochus relinquish all his claims in Europe. The peace settlement transferred Europe to the Romans and barred Antiochus from retaining those possessions.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: After Antiochus's overthrow, Roman commissioners arranged the division of territories in Asia. The regions on this side of the Taurus were assigned to Eumenes, while Caria and Lycia were assigned to the Rhodians; cities tributary to Antiochus were freed from tribute.

l: Publius Scipio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Antiochus offered to release Publius Scipio's son and to give Scipio a large sum of money in return for peace. Publius Scipio declined the money and advised Antiochus not to resist the Romans.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Hannibal the Carthaginian was named among those whom Antiochus was required to deliver to the Romans under the peace settlement.

l: Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Eumenes received the regions on this side of the Taurus and was given favorable treatment by the Roman Senate. Later, intercepted letters and accusations caused the Romans to suspect that he had allied with Perseus, so Caius was sent to observe his affairs and movements.

l: Rhodians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Rhodians received Caria and Lycia from the Roman commissioners. Later, their ambassadors came to Rome to answer accusations that Rhodes had secretly favored Perseus and weakened its friendship with the Romans; the Senate relieved their greatest fears but sharply rebuked some of their conduct.

l: Achaeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Achaian assembly was told that the Roman Senate was displeased by the demolition of the walls of Lacedaemon. The Achaians refused a present from Eumenes intended to defray the expenses of members of their senate, but renewed their league with Seleucus and accepted his present.

l: Attalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Attalus was associated with Asian princes who received an honorable reception at Rome because of their friendship and services to the Romans. Ambassadors who came with Attalus answered accusations successfully and returned home with honor.

l: Aetolians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Aetolian ambassadors seeking peace were required either to surrender their country to Rome or pay one thousand talents of silver. Their ambassadors later emphasized the services the Aetolians had performed for Rome, but the Senate sent them back without a favorable result.

l: Perseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Perseus was suspected of causing disturbances in Thessaly and among the Aetolians and of driving Abrypolis, king of Thrace, from his kingdom. The Senate declared war against him, expelled his ambassadors and the Macedonians from Rome and Italy, and later investigated alleged cooperation between Perseus and Eumenes.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: After the Senate declared war against Perseus, the Macedonians in Rome were ordered to leave the city immediately and Italy within thirty days.

l: Prusias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Prusias was portrayed as unworthy of royal dignity because of his sordid flattery of Rome. He dressed as a freed slave, called himself a Roman libertine, prostrated himself before the Senate, and received an answer suited to his excessive flatteries.

l: war against Antiochus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Roman Senate prepared for the expected war against Antiochus by seeking Greek support and warning that it would aid its friends and allies. The conflict ended after Antiochus accepted severe Roman conditions and surrendered substantial territory, resources, and persons.

l: peace with Antiochus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Antiochus sought peace after abandoning thoughts of war and offered concessions, but the Romans required extensive territorial, financial, and military terms. Peace was granted after he accepted those conditions.

l: peace treaty with Antiochus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The treaty required Antiochus to surrender Europe and territories on the Roman side of the Taurus, all elephants and long ships, fifteen thousand Euboean talents for war expenses, Hannibal, Thoas, and others, and twenty hostages chosen by the Romans.

l: Roman diplomatic embassies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Roman and foreign embassies addressed justice, alliances, peace, territorial claims, tribute, and military obligations. Roman representatives were sent to Alba, Asia, and other regions, while the Senate repeatedly received and judged ambassadors from Greece, Asia, Rhodes, and neighboring kingdoms.

l: Roman Senate, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Roman Senate confirmed peace terms, promised freedom and self-government to the Grecians, negotiated with Antiochus, imposed harsh terms on the Aetolians, and redistributed territories in Asia. It later declared war against Perseus, examined accusations against Eumenes and the Rhodians, and managed the reception and dismissal of numerous embassies.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: The Roman senate receives embassies concerning Ptolemy, Ariarathes, Demetrius, the Celtiberians, Carthage, and other foreign peoples, often imposing conditions or renewing alliances. The Carthaginians surrender hostages and arms but are later ordered to abandon Carthage and build elsewhere, prompting renewed resistance. The Aradians attempt to obtain Marathos, while the Marathonians appeal to them and are imprisoned. Scipio Africanus and other Roman ambassadors inspect Egypt and nearby regions, and later Bocchus secures Roman favor by helping Marius capture Jugurtha; Mark Antony and the Cretans also become involved in disputes over treaties and Roman commands.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Rome receives numerous foreign embassies and exercises authority over kings, cities, and allied peoples. Its officials and senate impose conditions involving hostages, arms, tribute, treaties, and obedience.

l: Roman Senate, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: The Roman senate orders the elder Ptolemy's ambassadors to leave Italy and directs that the confederacy with him be broken, while sending assurances to the younger Ptolemy. It commends Ariarathes, accepts crowns from Ariarathes and Demetrius, refuses to receive Isocrates and Leptines, and imposes severe conditions on the Carthaginians and Cretans. It also receives Bocchus into favor if he can prevail with Marius, and renews or confirms alliances with foreign peoples.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: The Carthaginians surrender themselves and their country to the Romans, send three hundred senators' sons as hostages, and deliver two hundred thousand weapons and two thousand engines. When ordered to abandon their city and build eighty furlongs from the sea, they lament, resist the decision, and renew the war.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Carthage is initially included in Roman assurances that the Carthaginians may retain their country, laws, temples, sepulchres, liberties, and estates. The Romans later decree that the city must be abandoned and destroyed, with a new settlement built eighty furlongs from the sea.

l: the Aradians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: The Aradians bribe Ammonius with three hundred talents to obtain the surrender of Marathos. They reject the Marathonian ambassadors' supplications, break the images they bring, trample them, and attempt to stone the ambassadors before senators send them to prison.

l: Marathonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: The Marathonians refuse entrance to the king's soldiers after observing that the Aradians have greater favor with the king. They send ten eminent elders to Aradus with a supplication and sacred images, but the ambassadors are attacked and imprisoned.

l: Scipio Africanus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Scipio Africanus travels with other Roman ambassadors to Alexandria and through Egypt, Cyprus, Syria, and other regions. The delegation's conduct earns honor, and it reconciles disputants, urges wrongdoers to act justly, restrains the obstinate, and refers difficult cases to the senate.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Egypt is examined by the Roman delegation, which notes its populousness, fertile country, the advantages of the Nile, its many cities, natural fortifications, and strategic capacity. The delegation judges that Egypt could become a vast empire if it had suitable rulers.

l: Alexandria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Alexandria receives Scipio Africanus and the other Roman ambassadors. Ptolemy shows them the palace, treasury, city, and the Pharos, while the delegation studies the city's situation and capacity.

l: Roman delegation to Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: The Roman delegation, including Scipio Africanus, inspects Alexandria, Egypt, Cyprus, Syria, and other regions. Its members prefer a spare and wholesome diet, disregard the king's luxury, and focus on strategic features; afterward they reconcile disputes, promote justice, renew leagues, and increase respect for Roman government.

l: Bocchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Bocchus, king of Libya, rebukes those who urge war against the Romans and sends commissioners to Marius seeking pardon and a league. He helps Marius seize Jugurtha, thereby buying his own safety and escaping Roman punishment.

l: Caius Marius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Marius directs Bocchus to send ambassadors to the senate concerning pardon and a league. With Bocchus's assistance, Marius lures Jugurtha under the pretense of discussing important business and has him seized and delivered to Lucius Sylla.

l: Jugurtha, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Jugurtha is summoned by Marius under the pretense of discussing matters important to them both. He is seized through this deception and delivered bound to Lucius Sylla.

l: Mark Antony, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Mark Antony makes a peace with the Cretans, which they observe for some time. The later dispute between Rome and the Cretans concerns accusations against them and the terms of their relationship with Rome.

l: Cretans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: The Cretans send thirty eminent ambassadors to Rome to defend themselves against accusations and seek restoration of their former amity and confederacy. The senate initially acquits them and declares them friends and confederates, but Lentulus Spinther reverses the decree; later the senate orders them to surrender their ships, three hundred hostages, Lasthenes, Panares, and four thousand talents of silver, leading to internal disagreement and sedition.

l: embassies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Embassies in this unit present gifts, request alliances, negotiate peace, defend cities, surrender prisoners or hostages, and seek relief from Roman commands. Some are favorably received, while others are rejected, threatened, imprisoned, or dismissed after severe demands.

l: alliances and confederacies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: The senate breaks off its confederacy with the elder Ptolemy, expresses goodwill toward the younger Ptolemy, and recognizes Ariarathes's goodwill. It also restores or renews alliances with foreign peoples, initially declares the Cretans friends and confederates, and considers leagues involving Bocchus.

l: Roman treaties and commands, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 23. Ambassadors came to Rome both from the yoonger and the
s: Roman agreements and commands require submission, hostages, weapons, tribute, military assistance, or relocation. The Romans order the Carthaginians to surrender hostages and arms and leave Carthage, impose extensive conditions on the Numantians and Termissians, and command the Cretans to surrender ships, hostages, named individuals, and silver.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: Alexander and his army crossed a waterless desert in Susiana, suffering intensely from heat, thirst, and dehydration. Alexander refused water brought for his own use because it was intended for the soldiers’ children, and after reaching the river Oxus he ordered fires and water-carrying parties to help those left behind. Alexander later encountered the Branchidae, descendants of people removed from Miletus by Xerxes and accused of betraying Miletus, and allowed the Milesians to decide their fate. He then ordered the Branchidae city destroyed, its inhabitants killed, and its walls and sacred groves completely removed.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: Alexander marched through a waterless desert with a band of light-armed men and suffered with his army from extreme heat and thirst. He refused to drink water brought for his own use because it had been intended for the soldiers’ children. After reaching the river Oxus, he ordered fires to guide those behind and directed the refreshed soldiers to carry water to their companions.

l: Alexander's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: Alexander's army crossed about four hundred furlongs without finding a lake or anything moist. Many soldiers became faint, some could not carry their arms or continue marching, and those who drank excessively vomited or died. A great part of the army was left behind before the force reached the river Oxus.

l: deserts of Susiana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: The deserts of Susiana were entered by Alexander and his light-armed men during a night march. They had no apparent water for four hundred furlongs, and their heated sands produced a mist that made the plain seem like a vast ocean.

l: the river Oxus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: Alexander reached the river Oxus about evening after the march through the desert. His arrival provided a place where the soldiers could refresh themselves and fill vessels with water for those still behind.

l: water, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: Water was scarce throughout the desert crossing, and some soldiers obtained small amounts through people familiar with the country. Two men brought water for their children in the army; one offered some to Alexander, but Alexander returned it and told him to give it to his children. After reaching the river Oxus, soldiers were ordered to carry water to their companions.

l: thirst and dehydration, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: The lack of water and intense heat caused the soldiers’ mouths and entrails to become parched and made their spirits and bodies faint. Their thirst led some to consume wine or oil, while excessive drinking caused vomiting, loss of strength, and death.

l: Alexander's march through the desert, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: Alexander's march through the desert began at night and was more tolerable because of the dew and cool air. After sunrise, scorching heat and drought made the march grievous, and many soldiers suffered or fell behind before Alexander reached the river Oxus.

l: the Branchidae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: The Branchidae inhabited a little town after having been removed from Miletus by the command of Xerxes. They spoke a broken language and welcomed Alexander, giving themselves and their city into his hands. Alexander later ordered them killed, and their city destroyed, because of their ancestors’ betrayal.

l: little town of the Branchidae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: The little town of the Branchidae was inhabited by people removed from Miletus by Xerxes. Alexander entered it with a select detachment while ordering the phalanx to surround its walls and raze it.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: Xerxes commanded the removal of the Branchidae from Miletus when he returned from Greece. The Branchidae were also described as having joined themselves with Xerxes after the violation of the Didymæus temple.

l: Miletus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: Miletus was the former home of the Branchidae, who were removed from it by Xerxes. The Milesians in Alexander’s army retained an old grudge against the Branchidae because their ancestors had been betrayed.

l: Milesians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: The Milesians in Alexander’s army bore an inveterate hatred toward the Branchidae because their ancestors had been betrayed by them. Alexander called the Milesians together and left the question of revenge or mercy to them, though they could not agree.

l: Didymæus temple, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: The Didymæus temple was described as a temple that the Branchidae had violated and whose contents they gave to Xerxes.

l: betrayal of Miletus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: The betrayal of Miletus was attributed to the ancestors of the Branchidae, who had betrayed the Milesians and were associated with Xerxes. The descendants of the Branchidae were punished for this act even though many had never seen Miletus.

l: destruction of the Branchidae city, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: Alexander ordered the Branchidae city to be razed to its foundations. Its walls were removed completely, and its sacred groves were cut down and rooted up so that no sign of the city remained.

l: the Branchidae massacre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. I.
s: The Branchidae massacre occurred after Alexander ordered the city surrounded and its inhabitants put to the sword. The disarmed Branchidae were killed indiscriminately, including men, women, and children, despite their prayers and entreaties.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: The unit describes Alexander’s suppression of a rebellion among the Sogdians and Bactrians, including the capture of several fortified cities and Cyropolis. His forces killed the male defenders, enslaved or carried away women and children, and subdued the remaining prisoners. The Asiatic Scythians then approached the river called Tanais in the text, identified in a note as the Iaxartes, and Alexander crossed it and defeated them. The unit also recounts Alexander’s decision to spare several Sogdian noblemen after being impressed by their courage and promises of loyalty.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: Alexander ordered his infantry to prepare scaling ladders and led campaigns against the rebellious cities. He captured and razed several towns, took Cyropolis by entering through the dry river channel, founded and populated a city, defeated the Asiatic Scythians at the Iaxartes, and spared several Sogdian noblemen after questioning them.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: The Macedonians in Scythia were surprised and killed by the rebelling barbarians. Alexander’s Macedonians captured the cities, entered Cyropolis, fought its defenders, and crossed the river to attack the Scythians.

l: Alexander's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: Alexander’s army captured five towns in two days and then took Cyropolis and the seventh city. It also crossed the river, defeated the Scythians, killed about a thousand of them, and took about one hundred and fifty prisoners.

l: Sogdians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: Many Sogdians joined the defection against Alexander after being solicited by those who had seized Bessos. Some Sogdian prisoners of noble birth impressed Alexander with their courage and were spared; those who returned home reportedly kept their countrymen obedient.

l: Asiatic Scythians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: The Asiatic Scythians came to the river because they heard that barbarians beyond it had revolted from Alexander. After taunting Alexander and opposing his crossing, they were defeated, with about a thousand killed and one hundred and fifty captured.

l: Craterus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: Alexander sent Craterus against Cyropolis and ordered him to fortify a camp near the city so that its defenders could not assist other cities. Craterus was wounded by darts and arrows during the fighting in Cyropolis.

l: Spitamenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: Spitamenes besieged the troops left in the castle of Patachades. Alexander sent Andromachus, Menedemus, and Caranus against him with cavalry and mercenaries.

l: Cyropolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: Cyropolis was the largest city and had been built by Cyrus, with higher walls and many defenders gathered inside. Alexander’s forces entered through the dry channel of the river, killed about eight thousand defenders, drove the remainder into the castle, and forced their surrender after one day because of thirst.

l: Gaza, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: Gaza is used as a comparison for the fortifications of another city that Alexander captured. The prisoners of that city were treated in the same manner as those at Gaza.

l: Tanais, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: The river called Tanais is presented as the river whose banks the Asiatic Scythians reached. A note explains that this was not the Tanais flowing into Lake Maeotis, but another river called the Iaxartes.

l: Iaxartes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: The Iaxartes is identified in a note as the river called Tanais in the narrative. Alexander crossed it with his army and defeated the Scythians on the farther bank.

l: rebellion of the Sogdians and Bactrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: The rebellion began when barbarians bordering the river surprised the Macedonian garrisons, killed them, and fortified the cities. Many Sogdians and some Bactrians joined the defection, allegedly because they feared Alexander or opposed his planned assembly of provincial governors at Zariaspa.

l: battle with the Scythians at the Iaxartes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: Alexander first used engines to wound and frighten the Scythians across the narrow river, then crossed with his army. His cavalry and light-armed troops broke the Scythians’ formation and put them to flight, killing about a thousand and capturing one hundred and fifty, including Satrices.

l: siege of Cyropolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: The siege began with orders to batter Cyropolis’s high walls using rams and other engines. Alexander then exploited the dry river channel to enter the city, after which the defenders fought fiercely before being driven from the marketplace and forced into the castle.

l: Scythian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: The Scythian army remained near the river, hurled darts across it, and insulted Alexander. After Alexander crossed, it initially resisted the Macedonian cavalry but was eventually surrounded, defeated, and forced into flight.

l: the seven cities of the country, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. III.
s: The barbarians were said to have fled into seven cities of the country. Alexander captured and razed five towns within two days, took Cyropolis after a siege, and captured the seventh city at the first assault, though the sources differed on whether that city surrendered or was taken by storm.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP, V,
s: Alexander marched again to the river Oxus and then led part of his army against the Sogdians, who had revolted and occupied forts and castles. He divided his army, reduced much of Sogdiana, and gathered his forces at Maracanda before sending commanders against remaining opponents and the Scythians. The Sogdians later took refuge on a steep, snow-covered rock where Oxyartes had placed his wife and daughters. Alexander's Macedonians climbed the rock by night, causing the defenders to surrender, and captured many women and children, including Oxyartes's family.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP, V,
s: Alexander marched again to the river Oxus and resolved to campaign against the Sogdians. He divided his army, led one part toward Maracanda, reduced revolted cities, and later assaulted the rock where the Sogdians had taken refuge. He promised safety to those who surrendered and offered rewards to the Macedonians who first climbed the rock.

l: Oxyartes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP, V,
s: Oxyartes had revolted against Alexander and placed his wife and daughters in the rock as an apparently impregnable refuge. His nine-year-old son was also captured there after the defenders surrendered.

l: Sogdians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP, V,
